title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
Page 262 finishes the case a = 10 of a series of particular theorems. For a prime q = 2p+1 it says which of 10^p − 1 or 10^p + 1 is divisible by q:
- q ≡ ±1, ±3, ±9, ±13 (mod 40): 10^p − 1.
- q ≡ ±7, ±11, ±17, ±19 (mod 40): 10^p + 1.
In modern terms this is the Legendre symbol (10/q) = (2/q)(5/q).

§32, the 'Theorema generale', states the rule behind all the tables. Take any a and a prime 2f+1, and suppose we know whether a^f ∓ 1 is divisible by 2f+1. Then the same sign holds for every prime 2p+1 = 4an ∓ (2f+1). By Euler's criterion this says (a/q) depends only on q modulo 4a and is unchanged under q → −q (mod 4a). That is Euler's form of quadratic reciprocity, stated here without proof.

§33 (f = 0): primes q ≡ ±1 (mod 4a) always divide a^p − 1. This is formally the trivial 'prime' 1.

§34 (f = 1): if 3 divides a − 1, then primes q ≡ ±3 (mod 4a) divide a^p − 1. If 3 divides a + 1, they divide a^p + 1.

§35 is a scholion: the tables can be extended using the problem that follows.

§36 poses that problem: decide, for given a and prime q = 2p+1, which of a^p ∓ 1 is divisible by q. The solution:
- List the p nonzero quadratic residues mod q.
- If a is a residue, a^p − 1 is divisible by q; if a is a non-residue, a^p + 1 is.
- This is Euler's criterion. The proof given covers only the residue direction: a ≡ x² (mod q) gives a^p ≡ x^{2p} ≡ 1 by Fermat. The proof concludes on the next page.

Purpose: a mechanical way to produce the residue-class tables (a = 11 etc. follow) and to support the general theorem empirically.
errors: The a = 10 table is fully correct: each class matches (2/q)(5/q).
§32 implicitly needs 2f+1 and 2p+1 not to divide a. Without that, neither a^p − 1 nor a^p + 1 is divisible. The theorem is also asserted without proof; it is equivalent to quadratic reciprocity.
§34 omits the case 3 | a. There a^1 ∓ 1 is not divisible by 3 for either sign, so the corollary gives no information.

§36 asserts that non-residues give a^p + 1. The argument (completed on p. 264) proves only that residues give a^p − 1. The converse needs a counting argument: x^p ≡ 1 has at most p roots, and a^{2p} ≡ 1 forces a^p ≡ ±1. Euler supplied this elsewhere, but it is a gap here.
The solution tacitly assumes q does not divide a.

ideas.what: Table of the residue classes mod 40 for which 10^p ∓ 1 is divisible by the prime 2p+1
ideas.where_published: E557 itself; related tables in E552 (Opuscula analytica I, 1783)

ideas.what: (a/q) depends only on q mod 4a and is invariant under q → −q
ideas.modern_name: Euler's formulation of the law of quadratic reciprocity
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured), proved by Gauss in 1796/1801; Legendre gave the symbolic form
ideas.where_published: E552 'Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos' (Opuscula analytica I); earlier statements in E164 and related papers

ideas.what: a is a quadratic residue mod q exactly when q divides a^{(q−1)/2} − 1, otherwise a^{(q−1)/2} + 1
ideas.where_published: E262 'Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta' (1761); E449

deep.surprise_reason: The page restates well-known material: Euler's form of quadratic reciprocity and Euler's criterion, both documented in standard histories (Weil, Lemmermeyer). The tables are correct and routine.
transcription_corrections: Page 263, first line: the '[?]' sign is ambiguous. Given 'prouti siue a−1, siue a+1', the sense is 'either a^p − 1 or a^p + 1 respectively'. The printed sign appears to be a single combined sign; it should be read as a^p ∓ 1 matching the two cases.
§32: the formula in the print reads 2p+1 = 4an ∓ (2f+1), consistent with the transcription.
